aevo-all.title: AEVO trainer aptitude: orientation and the practical part of the exam
aevo-all.description: Four lessons framing the practice questions. The first two set out what the examination rests on: the Ausbilder-Eignungsverordnung with its four Handlungsfelder, and the adjacent statutes that recur across all four. The last two are deliberately NON-QUIZZED background on the practical part of the examination - presenting or actually carrying out a training situation, and the Fachgespräch that follows. That part cannot be represented as a multiple-choice question, so it appears here as text. Note: unofficial practice material, not legally reviewed, and no substitute for your own chamber's information sheet.

aevo-u1.title: Orientation: the regulation, the Handlungsfelder, the exam structure

aevo-u2.title: The practical part - background guidance (not quizzed)

aevo-l0.title: What the AEVO requires - and how the examination is structured

aevo-l0-s1.title: A regulation with nine sections - and a competence profile in four fields
aevo-l0-s1.body:
The Ausbilder-Eignungsverordnung (AEVO, formally AusbEignV 2009) is short: nine sections and two certificate templates. It rests on § 30(5) of the Vocational Training Act (BBiG) and has applied since 1 August 2009. § 1 AEVO says whom it covers: trainers must prove they have acquired the vocational and work-pedagogical skills, knowledge and abilities for training in recognised training occupations under the BBiG - the only exclusion is training in the liberal professions.

The heart of it is § 2 AEVO. It defines vocational and work-pedagogical aptitude as "the competence to independently plan, deliver and monitor vocational training", and divides it into four Handlungsfelder that follow the course of an apprenticeship:

1. Examining the preconditions for training and planning the training
2. Preparing the training and participating in the recruitment of apprentices
3. Delivering the training
4. Concluding the training

§ 3 AEVO fills each field with competences - seven in field 1, six in field 2, nine in field 3, four in field 4. Read that section through once in full: it is the table of contents for the entire examination, and every exam task can be mapped onto one of its numbered items.

An important framing point: the AEVO is the same regulation nationwide, whether the examination is taken at a chamber of industry and commerce (IHK) or a chamber of crafts (HWK). What differs is the administering chamber, not the legal basis and not the Rahmenplan. § 6(2) AEVO further makes clear that the vocational and work-pedagogical part of a master-craftsman examination counts as equivalent proof.

Alongside the regulation there is a second, official reference point: the AEVO Rahmenplan, adopted as a recommendation of the main committee of the Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training on 20 June 2023 and published in the Federal Gazette (BAnz AT 14.07.2023 S2). It is not a statutory instrument but a recommendation - yet it is the nationwide quality standard for preparatory courses, and it translates every AEVO competence into concrete skills, knowledge and abilities plus "example content". It recommends 115 teaching hours and distributes them across the fields: 15 percent to field 1, 20 percent to field 2, 50 percent to field 3 and 15 percent to field 4. Field 3 is therefore clearly the centre of gravity - and this module's question pool follows the same weighting.

A warning about sources: the 2009 Rahmenplan (weighting 20/20/45/15 percent) is still reproduced as current on many websites. The authoritative version is the one of 20 June 2023, which expressly gives more weight to digitalisation, heterogeneity and sustainability.

aevo-l0-s2.title: Two exam parts, two separate hurdles - there is no averaging
aevo-l0-s2.body:
§ 4 AEVO governs how aptitude is proved. Paragraph 1 contains the sentence that shapes the whole exam strategy: "The examination is passed if each part of the examination has been assessed as at least 'sufficient'." There is therefore NO trade-off between the written and the practical part - an excellent practical part does not rescue an insufficient written one, and vice versa. Within one examination procedure, a failed examination may be resat twice, and a passed part can be credited.

The written part (§ 4(2) AEVO): "case-based tasks from all Handlungsfelder", and the examination "should last three hours". The regulation says no more than that. How the chambers implement it is set out in their information sheets: in practice 80 case-based, closed-form ("programmed") tasks in 180 minutes, answered by ticking boxes. Each task offers several proposed solutions, at least one of which is correct; where more than one is correct, the number is stated, and the all-or-nothing principle applies - the task counts as correct only if ALL correct options are marked. There is no supplementary oral examination for an insufficient written performance. Per the information sheets, the pass mark is 50 out of 100 points. Delivery is increasingly digital (tablet or notebook) rather than on paper. Uncommented statutory texts are generally permitted; the tasks are, however, designed so that they can in principle be solved without looking anything up.

The practical part (§ 4(3) AEVO): "the presentation of a training situation and a Fachgespräch with a total duration of at most 30 minutes". The presentation should not exceed 15 minutes; the selection and design of the training situation must be explained in the Fachgespräch; and "instead of the presentation, a training situation may also be carried out in practice". The next two lessons cover this.

Special case: under § 4(4) AEVO, in agriculture and home economics the practical part consists of carrying out a training situation plus a Fachgespräch with a total duration of at most 60 minutes.

What this module is NOT: there is no official, public AEVO question catalogue. The questions here are our own synthesis from the AEVO, the BBiG, the adjacent statutes and the Rahmenplan. They cannot reproduce the 80 real tasks, and they replace neither a preparatory course nor your own chamber's information sheet.

aevo-l1.title: The statutes that recur across all four Handlungsfelder

aevo-l1-s1.title: The BBiG is the real subject matter
aevo-l1-s1.body:
The AEVO describes competences but itself names almost no legal consequences. The legal consequences are in the Vocational Training Act (BBiG) - which is why case-based tasks from all four Handlungsfelder regularly converge on a BBiG provision. It pays to learn these provisions as a small map, ordered by the course of an apprenticeship.

Before training may happen at all (BBiG part 3): § 27 suitability of the establishment, including the appropriate ratio of apprentices to skilled workers and the saving clause in paragraph 2 for companies that cannot deliver all the content. § 28 separates taking on apprentices (personal suitability only) from training them (personal and professional suitability), and governs the appointment of a trainer and digital mobile training in paragraph 2 and the assisting skilled worker in paragraph 3. § 29 defines personal, § 30 professional suitability.

At contract formation (BBiG part 2): § 10 the contract, with the important paragraph 4 (a defect in entitlement does not affect validity) and paragraph 5 (consortium training). § 11 the contract record - twelve mandatory details, text form, without undue delay and at the latest before training starts. § 12 void agreements: restraint of trade, compensation for the training, contractual penalties, exclusion or flat-rating of damages. § 36 the application for registration in the register - without undue delay, and later a condition for admission to the examination.

During the training: § 13 apprentices' duties (eight items, including the training record). § 14 training providers' duties - systematic delivery, training personally or expressly commissioning a trainer, free training means, requiring school attendance, character development and protection from endangerment, reviewing the training record, and only training-purposive tasks appropriate to physical strength. § 15 release from work and crediting of time. §§ 17-19 the allowance: appropriate, rising at least annually, minimum rates for companies not bound by collective agreement, due date, continued payment, extra work. § 20 probation (at least one, at most four months). §§ 21-24 termination, dismissal, damages, continued employment. § 25 non-derogability - the provision that strikes down every agreement to the apprentice's disadvantage.

At the end: § 16 the company's training certificate (simple as mandatory content, qualified only on request). §§ 37-48 the examination regime, of which the most exam-relevant are § 37 (resits, freedom from fees, translations), § 43 admission, § 45 early admission and the external-candidate route, § 48 the interim examination. And § 8 - shortening on joint application, extension on the apprentice's application.

A pattern that carries a lot of weight in exam tasks: for every scenario, ask first WHO may or must act here (the company, the apprentice, the chamber, the works council), and ONLY THEN what the substantively correct answer is. A great many mistakes arise not on the substance but on competence - for instance where a company shortens a training period itself when only the chamber can do so.

aevo-l1-s2.title: The adjacent statutes: JArbSchG, BetrVG, AGG - and where they surface in the fields
aevo-l1-s2.body:
The Rahmenplan names them expressly as legal framework conditions, and the written examination picks them up regularly. What matters is not detailed knowledge of each whole statute but the provisions that actually trigger decisions in day-to-day training.

Youth Employment Protection Act (JArbSchG) - relevant to all apprentices under 18; § 15(3) BBiG refers to it expressly. The practically relevant limits: § 8 at most eight hours a day and 40 hours a week (exceptions up to 8.5 hours in paragraphs 2 and 2a). § 9 release for vocational school, no deployment before lessons starting earlier than 9 a.m., crediting against working time, no loss of pay. § 10 release for examinations and for the working day immediately before the written final examination. § 11 rest breaks: at least 30 minutes for more than 4.5 up to 6 hours, at least 60 minutes for more than 6 hours, never more than 4.5 hours without a break. § 19 holiday, graded by age at the start of the calendar year: 30 working days (not yet 16), 27 (not yet 17), 25 (not yet 18). § 23 the ban on piecework and pace-dependent work, with the narrow exception in paragraph 2 for group work. §§ 32-33 the initial medical examination before employment begins (within the last 14 months, with the certificate on file) and the first follow-up examination after a year. § 21a permits deviating rules only by collective agreement.

Works Constitution Act (BetrVG) - Handlungsfeld 2 requires taking account of the participation and co-determination rights of employee representatives. The three core provisions: § 96 promotion of vocational training, and determining training needs at the works council's request. § 97 consultation on facilities and measures, with genuine co-determination in paragraph 2 where company measures change employees' duties so that their knowledge no longer suffices. § 98 the one that matters most to trainers: paragraph 1 co-determination on the delivery of in-company training measures, paragraph 2 the right to object to the appointment of a person charged with vocational training, or to demand their removal, where they lack personal or professional - in particular vocational and work-pedagogical - suitability or neglect their duties. Add to that the youth and apprentice representation and, on recruitment, § 99 BetrVG.

General Equal Treatment Act (AGG) - Handlungsfeld 2 speaks of selecting apprentices "also taking account of their diversity", and the Rahmenplan requires selection procedures "taking account of the General Equal Treatment Act" and the GDPR. § 1 names the protected characteristics, § 6(1) no. 2 expressly covers persons employed for their vocational training and sentence 2 covers applicants, § 7 contains the prohibition of disadvantage, § 11 prohibits a discriminatory advertisement, and § 15 governs compensation and damages.

A memory aid for the exam: the JArbSchG concerns day-to-day delivery (Handlungsfeld 3) and contract preparation for minors (field 2); the BetrVG and the AGG almost always concern field 2 - preparing and recruiting.

aevo-l2.title: The practical part: presentation or live delivery

aevo-l2-s1.title: What the regulation requires - and what you therefore have to decide
aevo-l2-s1.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed.

§ 4(3) AEVO is the entire legal framework for the practical part, and it is four sentences long: "The practical part of the examination consists of the presentation of a training situation and a Fachgespräch with a total duration of at most 30 minutes. For this the candidate selects an occupation-typical training situation. The presentation should not exceed 15 minutes. The selection and design of the training situation must be explained in the Fachgespräch. Instead of the presentation, a training situation may also be carried out in practice."

From this follow four decisions you have to make before the exam day - and that nobody makes for you:

FIRST: presentation or live delivery? The regulation offers both as equally valid options. In a PRESENTATION you set out a training situation before the examination board; the board stays the board and takes on no role - it is your audience. In a LIVE DELIVERY you actually carry out the training situation with a person in the apprentice's role. Who that person is depends on the chamber: some chambers expressly require you to bring someone yourself (your own apprentice, a colleague, someone from your private circle), while others let a board member take the role. This is the single most important point to check in your own chamber's information sheet before you plan.

SECOND: which training situation? The topic must be drawn from the training framework plan of the occupation for which you hold professional suitability; a topic from your current occupational work is also permitted. Purely company-specific or general-education topics that cannot be derived from a training framework plan or from the AEVO are not. Important: "training situation" is BROADER than "instruction". The trainer's whole range of action is eligible - a teaching-and-learning unit on a specific objective, but equally an appraisal, feedback or critical conversation, a learning-needs conversation, a conversation about outstanding performance or about misconduct, briefing an assisting skilled worker, agreeing a project with the vocational school, planning a training phase, or selecting a company task as a learning project. Conversations work for both options and are frequently underrated.

THIRD: the time cut. 15 minutes for the presentation or delivery, at most 30 minutes in total including the Fachgespräch. It need not be to the minute - in chamber practice a coherent performance may deviate by one or two minutes - but the overall 30 minutes must be observed. So plan a clean ending rather than content that only fits the time if everything goes perfectly. For a live delivery this means concretely: choose a segment that genuinely reaches a conclusion within the 15 minutes. Some chambers expect the underlying training unit to be one that would take at least around 45 minutes in real workplace practice, of which you show a section.

FOURTH: a written concept. Many chambers require an orientation form or a declaration about the training situation in advance, often to be handed in on the day of the written examination - so the board can prepare. Beyond that they recommend working out a concept covering the didactic and methodological design. Note the difference: the orientation form is usually mandatory, whereas the detailed concept serves your own preparation, as a rule does not feed into the assessment, and often need not be shown to the board.

The single most common mistake: presenting the training company, its products, or an overview of various training methods. What is required is a CONCRETE training situation - one in which you become visible as the person acting.

aevo-l2-s2.title: Option 1 - presentation: a structure that holds up
aevo-l2-s2.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed.

The presentation should show that you can PLAN, DELIVER and MONITOR a training situation - exactly the three verbs from § 2 AEVO. A structure that makes those three steps visible almost always holds up:

1. A brief introduction of yourself and the topic, with your timing. Two sentences, not a company presentation.

2. Starting situation and audience analysis (the AS-IS). Who is the apprentice, in which year of training, what prior knowledge do they bring, what learning prerequisites and individual particularities exist? Where does the situation take place, when, for how long, under what conditions? This is the anchor against which every subsequent decision is justified.

3. Placement and reference to the training framework plan. Which position of the training regulation are you working on? Where does this situation sit in the company training plan? One sentence is enough - but it has to be there, because reference to the training regulation is a fixed assessment criterion.

4. Objective formulation (the TO-BE). A lot is decided here. Formulate an operationalised fine-grained objective: observable end behaviour, conditions, assessment standard. Name the learning domain and, where sensible, the objective level. For conversation-based situations, a clearly formulated conversation goal takes the place of the learning objective.

5. Choice of method WITH justification. Not just "I use a learning assignment" but why: objective, learning domain, stage of training, learning prerequisites, framework conditions, learning venue. Name one rejected alternative and say why it fits less well here - this is one of the most effective points in the whole presentation, because it shows weighing-up rather than memorisation.

6. Course of the situation. Describe the interaction between trainer and apprentice step by step, not just the list of topics. Where do you activate the apprentice? Where do you let them plan, decide and check for themselves? The Rahmenplan expressly highlights "learning-process guidance" in HF 3.4 - the more your description shows accompaniment rather than demonstration, the better it holds.

7. Media and aids, with the function of each justified. Bring everything you need yourself; chambers generally provide a whiteboard, flipchart, pinboard and projector. Your own laptop is your risk - technical failures and the resulting overrun are at your expense. PowerPoint is NOT prescribed: prepared flipchart sheets or pinboard cards are treated as equivalent in the assessment and never fail technically.

8. Motivation and transfer. What do you connect to in order to generate interest? And what happens after the situation - performance check, documentation in the training record, transfer to the next task?

9. Securing and checking success. How do you establish whether the objective has been met? Here the operationalised objective from step 4 pays off directly: a verifiable objective supplies its own performance check.

One methodological particularity you need to know: some chambers expressly EXCLUDE the classic conventional methods - the four-step method and the question-and-answer teaching conversation - as the subject of the "presentation" option, and instead expect the depiction of a longer, self-directed training unit, as a rule described using the model of the complete action (inform - plan - decide - carry out - check - assess). For the live-delivery option those same chambers apply the reverse: there the four-step method is the standard case in industrial/technical occupations. This is chamber practice, not an AEVO requirement - check it in your own information sheet, because it governs your entire choice of topic.

aevo-l2-s3.title: Option 2 - live delivery: what actually has to become visible
aevo-l2-s3.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed.

In a live delivery, the point is not that the task succeeds but that YOUR action as a trainer becomes visible. The examination board is watching you, not the workpiece.

A robust sequence where the objective is psychomotor (typical for industrial/technical occupations, classically with the four-step method):

STEP 1 - Prepare. Workstation, material and tools are ready before the clock starts. Greeting, establishing contact, connecting to prior knowledge, stating the objective clearly and in one sentence, explaining the point of the activity within the work process, giving safety instructions. This step is the one most often cut short under time pressure - and its absence is immediately noticeable.

STEP 2 - Demonstrate and explain. Slowly, in comprehensible sub-steps, naming the key points and the typical sources of error. Separate talking from showing where doing both at once overloads. Mind the sight lines: the apprentice must be able to see what you are doing.

STEP 3 - Imitate and explain. The apprentice performs the task AND explains what they are doing as they go. That simultaneous explaining is the real diagnostic core of the method: it surfaces comprehension errors, not just execution errors. You intervene only where safety or substantive correctness requires it - and let errors that carry learning value stand for the moment.

STEP 4 - Practise and consolidate, with a performance check. Independent repetition, a check against the objective stated in step 1, feedback following the feedback rules, an outlook on transfer into everyday work, and documentation.

Where the objective is cognitive (typical for commercial occupations), the four-step method is usually replaced by the question-and-answer teaching conversation: you lead through questions and the apprentice works out the solution themselves. The standard is the same - clarity of objective, activation, securing success.

If you carry out a CONVERSATION (learning-needs, appraisal, feedback or critical conversation), a distinct but equally clear structure applies: set a comfortable frame and name the occasion, disclose the goal of the conversation, first ask for the apprentice's self-assessment, then place your criteria-based observations alongside, work through the divergences together, reach a verifiable agreement with a date, and announce a follow-up. Speak about behaviour rather than the person, and open descriptively rather than judgementally.

What the board typically watches in a live delivery: greeting and entry into the topic; communication with the apprentice - were they activated and motivated for the topic; clear formulation of the objective; presentation and justification of solution alternatives; coherence of the pedagogical approach; fit of the methodological/didactic approach; handling of the media used; securing of success; observance of the time frame.

Three practical points that regularly cost time in the exam: first, working materials - bring everything yourself, and avoid time-consuming demonstrations of software or media, which do not match the purpose of the examination. Second, the apprentice's role - clarify in advance, chamber by chamber, whether you have to bring a person; if so, brief them honestly (they should react normally, not act, and not be unusually good). Third, the segment - choose a situation that genuinely reaches a conclusion in 15 minutes, rather than the most interesting but unfinished part of a larger task.

aevo-l3.title: The Fachgespräch: structure, assessment, and an exam-day checklist

aevo-l3-s1.title: What the Fachgespräch is - and what it expressly is not
aevo-l3-s1.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed.

The Fachgespräch follows immediately after the presentation or the live delivery. § 4(3) sentence 4 AEVO states its purpose in one sentence: "The selection and design of the training situation must be explained in the Fachgespräch." That is the key - and it is often misunderstood.

The Fachgespräch is NOT a general theory examination. It is not the board's opportunity to test knowledge detached from your situation. The starting point and basis remains the training situation you chose; the questions develop out of it. That is precisely why the choice of topic matters so much: a situation you command confidently, technically and pedagogically, carries the conversation. One you invented purely for the exam collapses in it.

What is typically asked can be sorted into four directions:

DIRECTION 1 - Why this way and not another? Justification of your choice of method, your objective formulation, your use of media. Which alternatives did you consider and reject? What would you do differently next time? Expect the question of how you would proceed if a framework condition were different - a weaker apprentice, less time, a different year of training, a group rather than one person.

DIRECTION 2 - Do you know other methods too? Knowledge of further training methods is presupposed and may be a subject of the conversation. You do not need to recite a list of methods, but you should be able to name two or three alternatives and say which objectives and learning domains they suit better.

DIRECTION 3 - Where does this sit legally? Questions on the training regulation and the statutory bases are expressly permitted, because placement within the legal framework is an assessment criterion: BBiG, JArbSchG, the training regulation and the training framework plan. You need not quote section numbers, but you should be able to say what your position follows from - and, for minors, know the limits of the Youth Employment Protection Act.

DIRECTION 4 - The wider context. How does the situation fit into the company training plan and into the work and business process? How do you check success, how do you document it, what happens next? And the three themes the 2023 Rahmenplan newly emphasises and which chambers expressly name as conversation subjects: digitalisation, sustainability, demographic change and heterogeneity.

On procedure: after the presentation or delivery the board may hold a short internal discussion, for which you leave the room. That is normal and not a signal. Following the Fachgespräch many boards give brief feedback and say whether the practical part has been passed. At some chambers the presentation/delivery and the Fachgespräch each count 50 percent towards the result of the practical part - so a weak Fachgespräch can eat up a good presentation.

aevo-l3-s2.title: What the examination board is listening for: the assessment criteria
aevo-l3-s2.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed. The criteria below come from published guidance issued by chambers of industry and commerce; they are chamber practice and vary in detail.

FOR THE FACHGESPRÄCH these questions are regularly applied:

- Was the problem, task or topic grasped and analysed?
- Goal orientation: were learning objectives formulated - and was their attainment checked?
- Are there solution alternatives, and is the chosen solution justified?
- Is the reference to the training regulation clear?
- Practice orientation: is the integration of the training situation into the company process apparent?
- Does the candidate possess vocational and work-pedagogical competence?
- Does the placement within the statutory framework succeed - BBiG, JArbSchG, training regulation, training framework plan?

FOR THE PRESENTATION, add: opening and self-introduction; description of the starting situation with audience analysis; grasp and analysis of the problem; clear formulation of the objective; presentation of solution alternatives with justification; coherence of the pedagogical approach; use of and handling of the chosen media; presentation technique - gesture, expression, language; observance of the time frame.

FOR THE LIVE DELIVERY, add: greeting and entry into the topic; communication with the apprentice - were they activated and motivated; clear formulation of the objective; presentation of solution alternatives with justification; coherence of the pedagogical approach; fit of the methodological/didactic approach; use of media; securing of success; observance of the time frame.

Read these lists across once: five criteria appear in all three, and they are therefore the real axis of the examination.

1. OBJECTIVE FORMULATION. A clearly formulated, verifiable learning or conversation objective. Anyone who stays vague here also loses ground at four other points.
2. JUSTIFICATION AND ALTERNATIVES. What is assessed is not the decision but its justification. There is almost never exactly one correct method - there is one you can relate to the objective, the stage of training and the framework conditions.
3. COHERENCE OF THE PEDAGOGICAL APPROACH. Do the starting situation, objective, method, course and performance check hang together logically? The most common break: a psychomotor objective paired with a purely cognitive method - or a performance check that tests something other than what the objective states.
4. REFERENCE TO THE TRAINING REGULATION AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK. One sentence on the position in the training framework plan, one on the applicable legal basis.
5. SECURING SUCCESS AND TRANSFER. How is attainment of the objective checked, and what happens next?

If you align your preparation with these five points and have a sentence ready for each, you can connect to any direction the Fachgespräch takes - including a question you did not expect.

aevo-l3-s3.title: Checklist: the weeks before, and the exam day
aevo-l3-s3.body:
GUIDANCE / BACKGROUND - this section is not quizzed.

FOUR WEEKS BEFORE
- Obtain your own chamber's information sheet and orientation form and read them in full. Check three points specifically: does the live-delivery option require you to bring your own person as the apprentice? Is the four-step method excluded as a subject for the presentation? When and how must the declaration about the training situation be submitted?
- Fix the training situation. Criterion: a situation from your real practice whose technical content you command confidently and which can be derived from a training framework plan.
- Decide between presentation and live delivery, and be able to justify the decision in writing.

TWO WEEKS BEFORE
- Write the concept: starting situation and audience analysis, reference to the training framework plan, operationalised learning or conversation objective, choice of method with justification AND one rejected alternative, course, media, performance check, transfer.
- Formulate one prepared sentence for each of the five core criteria.
- Be able to name two or three alternative methods, with the area each suits.
- Clarify the legal framework of your own situation: training regulation, the applicable BBiG provisions, and for minors the JArbSchG.

ONE WEEK BEFORE
- Run it twice under realistic conditions with a stopwatch. Only then cut - do not plan to cut in advance.
- Prepare an analogue fallback medium: prepared flipchart sheets or pinboard cards work without power and are assessed as equivalent.
- For a live delivery: brief the person in the apprentice role - react normally, do not act, do not be unusually good.
- Write a materials list and pack it. Bring everything you need yourself.

ON THE EXAM DAY
- Arrive early, look at the room and the media equipment, check sight lines and set-up.
- Bring the orientation form or declaration about the training situation, if not already submitted.
- In the conversation: hear the question out, think briefly, then answer. Follow every answer with one sentence of justification - "I chose X because Y".
- For a question you cannot answer confidently: say what you do know and name the limit, rather than guessing. Admitted uncertainty costs less than a wrong assertion.
- The board may step out of the conversation for a short internal discussion, or ask you to leave the room. That is procedure, not a verdict.

TWO ORGANISATIONAL POINTS TO CLOSE
- Under § 4(1) AEVO the examination is passed only if EACH part is at least "sufficient". An insufficient written part does not, as a rule, prevent you from sitting the practical part anyway - a failed examination may be resat twice within one examination procedure, and a passed part can be credited.
- Under § 5 AEVO, a certificate in accordance with annexes 1 and 2 of the regulation is issued for a passed examination, and with it the vocational and work-pedagogical skills, knowledge and abilities within the meaning of § 30 BBiG are proved. The AEVO knows no refresher or renewal obligation - the proof is valid indefinitely.
